Review after completing the first week: 

There's a lot to appreciate in Demonschool. You can feel the Into the Breach influence in the tactics sections - they are puzzles that reward efficiency, spatial mindfulness, and thoughtful planning. It's the type of experience that would be enough to support a game on its own. But I really appreciate everything built around it and the fact that it has a time-based story. It could feel good to play just tactics sections endlessly so it helps to have a deadline!

The graphics and music are great. The music is original and engaging. I imagine it would be a great listen even stripped of the context. Graphically, everything is well crafted, but I want to give a shout out to the transitions which are where that Persona comparison might be especially relevant.

The writing could certainly be more efficient, but its personality stands out. Every character so far is endearing, the Scooby-Doo mystery vibes are fun, and after experiencing the first weekend, I have a feeling that a lot of the best bits of writing and fun little games within the game are yet to come. 

It feels like a bit of a slow burn to show its full hand of mini-games, relationships, abilities, etc. and that feels like the right call so far. Personally, I'm at a moment where I'm a little oversaturated with chunky, full-brain mechanics and narrative games, so I appreciate that this one eases you in.

[h3] We've got a [b] hot [/b] video game over here [/h3]

I'll start off by saying I'm not a big 'tactics' person, and I only have a passing familiarity with the likes of Persona, Shin Megami Tensei, or Soul Hackers. If you're looking for a review that is able to dig into those games in some sort of swing towards comparative literature, keep looking.

Despite my failings on that front, I do think that enables me to give this a stamp of approval from another perspective: the casual. Demonschool presents a seemingly lived-in universe within which you not only get to pop in and out of bite sized puzzle-battles, but also get to hang out and interact with 'people' that have some humanity in their writing. If you're someone that can get a chuckle out of some quick witted dialog, Demonschool has a Thanksgiving-meal-worth of delights. Demonschool's fights will also hit if you are someone that frequents daily puzzle websites, has a favorite release of picross, or enjoys a board game or two.

Separate from those features both mechanical and talkative, the game is wrapped within a confident art style. If you have browsed the screenshots on the Steam page, you will have a great idea of whether or not you [i] want to see more of that. [/i] These striking visuals are bolstered by a first-in-class soundtrack with earworms abound. 

My dog is somewhat annoyed with me as my attempts to mimic some of soundtrack's percussion closely mirror noises I employ to get his attention. He will have to exercise patience with me for as long as Demonschool has mine. If the handful of hours I have between the demo and the final release are indicative to the experience as a whole, it'll be a while.

Every battle you encounter has a turn limit in case you want to reach 3 stars, AKA, the maximum rank in the combat, if you didn't win on the turn limit, you will not have the maximum rank, wich means less points you will receive, wich means you will take longer to buy the abilities in the shop, the game allows you to rewind the battle even if you beat it, so is not like if you fail it to do it on time you will never do it again. But, again, this isn't a strategy game like Devil Survivor (wich is the closest game with the gameplay of Demonschool), the game wants you to find the most precise and perfect solution for the battles.

Some might not care about this like i do, but some might find it a big issue, take this info in consideration if you want to buy the game.

The game has bugs like the reviewers said already, to the point that my game crashed in the middle of a battle, the music sometimes stops, etc etc, i assume the game will get a patch day 1. And the spanish translation is heavily influenced on the mexican language, so if you are not from there, you can have difficulties understanding what it says, and is also sometimes a direct translation of the english script, let's just say that i switched to the english translation in 30 minutes, it clearly needs to be fixed (and specify this is the LATAM Spanish, and not "Spanish" in general like the game says)

This is less of a full review and more of a list of pointers to help you decide if the game is for you or not:

- Gameplay is split between a very simple "school life" part where you talk to NPCs and get new skills and passive buffs and the combat itself. These two aspects are well balanced and they switch up often enough that i was never bored with either one.

- Combat is a lot of fun, if you've played Tactical Breach Wizards it's surprisingly similar in that each fight is less about surviving your enemies (you can undo your actions infinitely so long as you don't end your turn) and more about finding ways to kill as many of them in as few moves as possible. More puzzle, less tactics if you will.

- I can't say much regarding the social link stuff yet as i haven't seen much of it, but it seems like you can stumble upon optional events that allow you to choose which character you want to bond with. Since the world is segmented into tiny instanced areas, these events are really easy to find.

- Story and writing so far are good, though the game doesn't take itself too seriously (at least for the first couple hours). It did make me laugh out loud a couple times, and the characters have fun chemistry.

I'm having a lot of fun with this so far, recommended.

(Note: this is a tentative review after playing the demo and the first week of the main story. I'll update my thoughts once I beat the game. Probably. Maybe.)
[i]Demonschool[/i] does a lot of things right from the get-go. The graphics are incredible, the music slaps, and the combat system is exactly what I enjoy. I'm a huge fan of RPGs where every encounter is a puzzle, like [i]Might and Magic: Clash of Heroes[/i] or [i]Into the Breach[/i], and this game scratches that exact itch. The music shifting into high-gear between the planning & action phases while your characters are kicking ass is a nice touch as well. 
The story side is where the game is admittedly the weakest. It's clearly trying to channel the vibes of the original [i]Persona[/i] games, but with a much more humorous tone, and, if you enter into a comparsion with [i]Persona 2[/i] story-wise, prepare to get left in the dust. The character writing is not to my tastes, but not anything I can complain about. My real complaint is that the script is much in need of an editing pass. This was something I noticed in the demo, but sadly it wasn't fixed. There are many, many sentences that are missing an obvious comma, which makes dialogue painful to read at times, with an awkward flow. 
Despite my complaints, I would give [i]Demonschool[/i] a strong recommendation to anybody who's interested in puzzle-y, tactical RPGs, or fans of the [i]Persona[/i] series (the old or the new). If, however, you're coming for a strongly written, deep story, you'll probably end up disappointed. Unless, of course, the story gets better in the coming weeks and I leave with my mind blown.

I was pretty sure I was going to love Demonschool from the first time I heard about it-- after all, I'm in love with so many of the things that it was influenced by, from giallo movies to Sega Saturn games to SMT: Devil Survivor (to Radiant Historia, which probably wasn't an actual influence? But it might be?). But it was still an amazing surprise to fall in love with this game by the end of the first battle. Everything meshes really well, from the character designs to the 2D sprites on a 3D field to the incredible soundtrack (which I'm going to go and buy after I write this review). It's easy to get overwhelmed by the aesthetic in all the best ways! Everything is acid coloured, the banter between characters is bright and witty, and the way the settings fly apart at the start of battles was of particular note for me.

Just... overall I can't stop gushing about this game. It's as though a game got made with me specifically in mind! You may feel different, because you're not me, but you might be like me, and if so, you're going to love this one. It's just dripping with style, and it's easy to read all of the Necrosoft team's love and care that went into making it.

Where Into the Breach uses a system where you can see what your enemies will do and plan around it, Demonschool does a neat thing where you can build combos by using action points to move your four characters as you like. So sequencing can help move enemies around, build lines of enemies to attack, and leave characters in better placement for the next move. Rewinding while I plan is a great feature, and then seeing all the choices unfold in real-time is cool.

So far, the core story has good character dialogue, interesting characters, people who remind me of some of the oddballs I hung out with in college. I'll say more here when I've played more. 

The NPC dialogue is tiny, cute, limited. It's not as fleshed out as, say, big typical JRPG, but it adds flavor. My routine is to talk to everyone early in the week in-game and then to mainly focus on story events or what shows up in the travel menu. 

By the way, the tool-tips (travel menu, info displayed in battle, status menus) are all gorgeous, responsive, and informative. I keep noticing little details in the UI as I play - like, in combat, seeing how many AP a character will use the next time they act represented as a little number in the bottom left. 

So if I had to sum all this up so far, I'd say Demonschool is kind of like if a game advanced the indie tactical combat threads of the last ten years (as seen in Into the Breach and similar), connected all that with a comedy-horror coming of age story that is a bit Buffy the Vampire Slayer and a lot of other horror/comedy media, and brought it all together really well.

Writing a little pre-review situation here after spending a few hours playing it because I have been absolutely floored by the audiovisual experience on offer, here. This is genuinely one of the most beautiful games that I've ever played. The spritework is immaculate, and the way that they've constructed the world is filled with so much flavor and intent. And the music! I'm having a good time with the rest, but it's genuinely worth playing for that alone. Will write more when I've played more.
Here is a rare thing: a game with texture, atmosphere, and swagger; roiling with a giddiness that, less than an hour in, has me fully invested in seeing where this all goes.

The way the grid battles play out feels unique, and the battles, so far, are fast paced, preventing the bogged down slog feeling that often accompanies tactical games.

The art and music are also great, and I find the quirky characters intriguing. Moving around the different areas of the island between battles is fast and easy, making it so it never feels like there's a risk of missing something.

The overall atmosphere is light, with a lot of humor, and you can see a lot of the creators' personalities and interests coming through. It's a fun world to hang out in.

So far:

Demonschool is very obviously inspired by the older Persona games (1-3) in its setting and visual style. The art seems to be one of the high points, so far. On the other hand -
The storytelling feels quite clunky. You're thrown on a ship sailing a pink sea (?) with no context given, and asked to pick a friend to make. The game does not make it clear that who you speak to is locked as your companion for the early game, passing up your opportunity to interact with the others. The dialogue is - not great, honestly. There are frequent grammatical errors (like missing commas) and it feels stiff and a bit amateurish.

That said, I do recommend the game, if tentatively, to fans of the older Persona titles. For those unfamiliar with Persona 1-3: Maybe try playing P2: Innocent Sin or P3 first, for more compelling writing and characters.

My experience with Demonschool has been one of pure enjoyment as I've gone through. The story is an entirely comedic jaunt onto an island where demons roam free and everyone knows that the apocalypse is going to happen in a few weeks. You follow Faye, who is determined to stop the world from being overtaken by demons, which involves gathering and befriending innate demon hunters at her college, while making sure to appease the school administration enough to not get arrested for failing their "extracurriculars". The story has some dark eldritch horror, but it's never enough to strike fear into you because of the whimsical writing for the characters.

The gameplay is this weird mix of Fire Emblem and that one childhood game of unblocking the car. With a set grid, the player works to defeat enough enemies to be able to unlock the "seal" and close the demon realm by having a character reach the end of the map. I found it to be like a puzzle game of how to eliminate the most enemies with the limited actions points given each turn. It continues to engage me even after 20 or so battles, with how new enemies, new skills, and new party members become periodically available to me. 

A lot of the reviews I read before playing described it in reference to the Persona series, but beyond the mechanics of a time sensitive calendar system, a confidant/bond system, and the plot involving "another world", I would say that they did their own thing. The story seems to be railroaded where you have to progress the plot in order to move time forward. Normally this would ruin my experience if I were thinking of it as a Persona game, but that was mitigated through how sidequests and bonds were handled. Instead of limiting the player to only being able to progress bonds/sidequests with a small allotment of time you have to manage, you can choose to pursue any or none of them at your leisure. They really add to the experience of the game if you do them, but it hasn't made it that you can't progress the main plot if you choose not to! So if you don't like a particular character, you can flip them off and ignore them to your heart's content <3

To top it off, HANDS DOWN THE MOST GORGOUS ART DIRECTION I'VE SEEN!!! The transitions from normal to demon realm are so awesome, animations are fun and readable, and i'm in love with the graphic black the character designers went for!

Demonschool is an incredibly stylish tactics game about a school haunted by demons. Despite the creepy creatures you're fighting, the tone is more that of a saturday morning cartoon, edgy anime or a shlocky b-movie than anything properly scary. The combat revolves around pushing and pulling enemies around a grid, combining attacks between the different team members, and figuring out the optimal order of operations to clear as many enemies as possible off the board in each turn. You are allowed to rewind all actions and the battles are pretty short, so you're never many steps away from a perfect score. Every battle is like a little puzzle, with some unique elements to figure out, and there isn't just one way to solve it, there are randomised elements and it's about having a solid understanding of how it all plays together, a mix of tactics and improvisation. At the end of each turn, when you have all your actions locked in, you see them play out all at once, like a general sending troops into battle, in a dynamic and stylish display that would make XCOM blush with shame. 

It has luxuriously loungy music and a gorgeous visual style that feels like it is simultaneously retro and something unique and new. Every element seems incredibly well considered and crafted with care. The writing is sharp and I can already tell it has a lot of heart. If you are interested at all in the genre or grabbed by its themes, you should definitely give it a go.

Cautious recommendation. If I could give a sideways thumb I would. I hate to have to compare any game to Bloomtown: A Different Story, but this is the most similar game I can think of. While this has much stronger fundamentals than that game (and is therefore actually fun and gets a hopeful thumbs up), it falls victim to a lot of the same traps; namely, it leans heavily on sharing visual and thematic identity with Megami Tensei while changing the recipe enough to be unrecognizable.

If you're coming in as a Persona/Devil Survivor fan: Don't bother. You won't find that here.

The combat is largely original, more akin to Into the Breach than anything else. The emphasis on hitting turn targets massively biases viability towards all-out offense. There's hardly anything to plan or strategize for outside of battle, and most of your plotting will be about lining up targets within each battle given your limited moves. The battle system is fun, but it's barely an RPG - it's a tactics game. Again, don't be fooled by the Persona nod.

Exploration is practically nonexistent since this game borrows the Devil Survivor format of "choose a location and do a fight there". Not a mark against the game, but another place that this game deviates from the promise of getting to actually explore a demon world. It constantly feels like things are happening around the cast. The goal is "find a videotape" and you just click all the advance time events until you find the videotape; there's no work to be done on my part as the player besides battling through all the goons.

The characters are pretty funny. The energy can be best described as a cheesy B-movie. Everything is full of puns, gags, brick jokes, catchphrases, and absurdism. I love it, but I wish there was more genuine dialogue outside of the core cast - a lot of NPCs in town are things like "red bag wanter" who says one line of dialogue like "I want that red bag" or whatever and it makes the world around the party feel paper thin. The main characters (read: anyone with a portrait) are incredibly charming but that same charm is not reflected at all beyond them.

Maybe the Bloomtown comparison is uncharitable. This is a fine game with good atmosphere and a great combat system. But a Persona-like it is not, and I probably wouldn't have bought it if I knew that.

Combat aside, the pixel art is great, and the environments really nail the 90s-Giallo-via-Japan vibes. Characters are well-written and likable; the game definitely knows its influences, and is not afraid to give them tongue-in-cheek nods where appropriate. References and gags are peppered throughout, but in a way that is cute and doesn't overdo it.

And melding it all together is the soundtrack. The score of this game slaps; each day of the week has its own theme, and they're all earworms. Wednesday is my favorite. I went to make dinner with the game running just so I could keep listening.

Overall, this game is a must-grab for me. Wonderful game, by wonderful devs, who clearly put in the work to make something and managed to stick the landing. I'll be completing this (probably 100%ing it).

Unfortunately, we don’t live in such a world. Fortunately, you can buy Demonschool for $25 on Steam and pretend you do! 

Equal parts puzzle game and hangout game, Demonschool is a love letter to video games cooler and older than 99% of Fortnite players, made by developers who played those games when they came out, are on first name basis with the people who made them, started websites to celebrate them (shout out to InsertCredit.com), and understand these influences well enough to distill their essence into something new and beautiful.  A true triumph.

My biggest complains are mostly about the attention given to the companions, and the endings. 

All of the companions were really interesting, but I don't think they were given enough time. Why are only Namako, Destin, and Knute your soulmates, why weren't there more side quests for them? If Namako is your only girl soulmate, why can't you kiss her, but you can kiss Knute?

Especially since some of the companions felt like they were added just because? Henk is cool, I love a punk, and love it when people think about what a punk is. Varka I know literally nothing about other than that he went to prison for killing a possessed body, and loves cheese. Pangxie idk how to talk about him ngl. This game has big Nintendo DS energy, which is some high praise coming from me.

A couple points in case you're on the fence:
[list]
    [*]The screenshots on the store page at present show a pixelated font for dialogue - if you have bad eyes like me, rejoice because they've since replaced it with a much cleaner non-pixelated font in 1.0 
    [*]Fire Emblem or Final Fantasy Tactics this is not - the Tactics-RPG-y-ness hews closer to something like Into the Breach. You've got unlimited undo's per turn in your planning phase and it's much more about maximizing actions than creating busted character builds. That does not mean every encounter is some pre-defined puzzle with only one solution (as you might see other reviews intimate), you still choose which characters to deploy and what passive skills to equip. 
    [*]You don't need to stress about optimally planning out your schedule to build up relationships like a Persona game. Only the plot moves the clock forward, side quests and bonding activities can be done without worrying about missing out on something else. 
    [*]On the note of character bonding, it's more of a side dish than big back-of-the-box feature. Most characters have 3 bond events to play through and that's it. Think of it more like a small side quest chain starring that party member rather than a game-long investment in seeing their character grow. Edit for fuller thoughts now that I've finished the game: 

Demonschool is quite simply, a lovely game. I wanted to say “little” there, too, but one thing I was constantly struck by during my 42-hour playthrough (it’s pretty big, for an indie RPG!) was how generous the game feels. The cast of characters starts out small, but grows throughout the course of the game, with each addition offering some new twist on a familiar character class or a new class that might be entirely unique to them, plus a new set of companion quests for each one. Side activities (including side quests, but also little activities you can do around the game world) are similar, with new diversions popping up almost until the very end of the game

The result is a game that at times feels like it’s bursting at the seams, perhaps trying to do a little bit too much, but Necrosoft’s ambition pays off in spades, thanks to the game putting its focus on the things that matter most. There are some areas where the game could perhaps do with a little more variety (like perhaps another handful of enemy types, particularly for the later chapters, or a few more tracks on the otherwise great soundtrack), but the game rightly spends much of its time on its companions, which are the heart and soul of any good party-based RPG

Thanks to the large cast of characters and their unique skills (and some delightfully cool twists on the actual structure of battles in the last third or so), there’s still plenty of room to play in the game’s engaging, puzzle-like combat sandbox while letting the game hone in on its cast, which is probably its greatest strength. Your party members (and protagonist Faye) are far more fleshed out and realized than the rosters of many other tactical RPGs. Screentime for each of them is surprisingly well-balanced—even if a handful do have more important roles to play in the broader narrative than others—and most importantly, they’re distinctly characterized, too. Both in terms of character designs and character writing, each character’s personality shines brightly through the game’s snappy (and often rather funny) writing, with each of them feeling like they add something to the game as a whole (which is no mean feat for a game with fifteen distinct party members!)

Of particular note for me is the game’s general approach to queerness in its characters. A regular complaint I have with many RPGs featuring character bonding and romance is that queer characters often lack a certain je ne sai quoi in the portrayal of their queerness. To be queer is almost by definition to be at least a bit counter-culture, and in many mainstream RPGs that feature nods toward or surface-level queerness, something of this element is lost in attempts to make the game palatable to a wider, straight audience

That’s not the case for Demonschool, though. I have never played an RPG where I saw so much queerness I recognized, so many quirks of dress or attitude or patterns of courtship that I’ve known in others or embodied myself as a queer woman. This is especially, well, special to me as a lesbian long-frustrated by so many sapphic options in romance-featuring RPGs being at best bisexual to also appeal to straight men or, at worst, having their queerness removed (such as in BioWare’s Mass Effect 2, where the pansexual Jack is only available as a romance for a male protagonist)

And best of all, because all of these characters are so skillfully realized, their queerness never feels out of place or tacked on (as it does in other RPGs, like BioWare’s somewhat recent Dragon Age: The Veilguard or even the much-loved Baldur’s Gate 3 from Larian). Instead, in Demonschool, these characters are not queer in order to satisfy a desire for representation for representation’s sake or because it means extra publicity in the modern era, but rather because Demonschool’s cast reflects an understanding that queerness exists in the world and also an understanding of how queerness manifests in that world

All of this works especially well for the game’s (perhaps familiar, but nonetheless well-crafted) anti-authoritarian story in which a bunch of loveable weirdos (and even a freak or two) find family together and decide they have to make things better themselves in the face of corrupt authorities. In that sense, Demonschool is not necessarily innovative, but I’m of the view that well-told and -structured stories don’t have to innovate to be good or satisfying, and Demonschool pulls off both good and satisfying, with its stellar cast making for a wonderfully memorable experience

When I play a game and ultimately judge it, it is usually based on one big factor for me: does the game accomplish what it set out to do, regardless of its faults? 

For Demonschool, it absolutely does. Pretty much no game is perfect, but Demonschool is perfect in capturing the vibe it presents. The artwork, soundtrack, and gameplay all tie together to make a fun and nostalgic experience that I've been invested in for the past few days.

From a gameplay standpoint, this is a tactical RPG more in line with a puzzle game like Into the Breach and Tactical Breach Wizards, where the strategy lies in making the best choices per turn. I think this lends itself great to the "vibe" I mentioned as you can choose to either ace the fight using the fewest turns possible, or just cruise at your own pace.

For the story/other gameplay, I am a sucker for impending doom stories and I like the setting a lot. Character interactions are fun and everything makes sense within the logic of the world. The time-management is more there as just a way to give pacing to the plot, but there are a few side activities that you can do to boost your friendships and get bonuses.

Some of the fights can be a little repetitive (what RPG isn't like this) and I have run into a few bugs but nothing crazy.

Overall, I really dig this game and am fully invested into finishing it. 

I don't mean to use this review to bring up another subject, but I feel that people are hypercritical of games these days. They want every single thing to be perfect or be "worth the money", which is understandable since you want your money to go far. But at the same time, we should appreciate that games like this continue to be made. The amount of varied experiences I have had just this year from games that may be far from perfect are more memorable and engaging than any $70 game I have played this year. 

I hope games like this continue to be made. I have been playing video games as my main hobby since as long as I can remember, and being able to play passionate works like this is what makes video games so special to me.

As for the writing, it's going to be a taste thing at the end of the day, but I think this game does a good job of staying light and campy (think John Carpenter movies, and again, the Yakuza series). This game also avoids the problem of endless scenes of dialogue that seems to plague so many games these days. Everything in this game is snappy and to the point, and maybe that's the issue for some people.

Nearly 20 years after creating a Steam account, I've decided to write my first review.

Demonschool is a tactics RPG that stands on the shoulders of its predecessors and brings a big idea of its own that makes it triumphantly stand out in its genre. There are lots of ideas and lessons learned from the likes of Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Survivor(s), Black Matrix, and a litany of other tactics games but Demonschool brings in a neat, real-time element into the battle system that involves planning all of your actions in advance each turn and then watching them play out at once in a shower of biffs, bops, and some visual fireworks thrown in for good measure. During the planning phase you are able to reverse your decisions as much as you want so that you can keep experimenting with how you'd like your turn to play out until you're fully satisfied with the results. Battles are structured a little more like puzzles in that regard as you try to maximise your actions, especially if you are attempting to go for the entirely optional A-ranks. Also, there are instant restarts if you mess up and want to try again.

A lot of comparisons have been made to the Persona games and, at a surface level, I would agree. On the face of it, you are responsible for a Scooby Gang of university students that are solving an ever-growing mystery happening on the island that the story takes place; the closest parallels are both Persona 2 games and elements of Personas 3 and 4. There are also social elements that are a mixture of mandatory and optional but the similarities end there. Social elements are limited to short mini games that are over in a flash, followed by character-specific events at certain relationship thresholds that typically involve a short battle. 

I like the Persona games but their biggest sins are painful amounts of patronising narrative bloat and exposition. In contrast, Demonschool's narrative is concise and snappy - you are trusted to suspend an iota of disbelief, follow the story and just enjoy the ride through some brisk dialogue. That dialogue, of which, I'm impressed by - characters talk like the late teens of the nineties and early noughties; they joke, banter, have some endearingly stubborn and enthusiastically stupid thoughts and ideas, and the Whedon-esque quips and one-lines that plague contemporary dialogue simply aren't there. You will see lots of little charming touches like mini-reviews of real movies, and nods to weird and unusual horror stories. You will see dumb jokes that have ellicited plenty of laughs; an early laugh came from how nuanced weightlifting is and a later description of a lighthouse describes its purpose as "stops boats from bonking into the island". They are silly, innocent and charming and a far cry from dry, mis-fired grandeur, dumbed-down, over-explained stories or overt references to, or outright repetition of, memes. Demonschool gets to the point quickly and concisely and it serves to speed up the pace of tangible progression far more than its peers.

Fundamentally, unless you're a joyless grouch then you'll have a good time with Demonschool. There's enough friction for it to feel like a videogame enjoyer's videogame without ever feeling like you're going to get stuck. There's a fun story with some light-hearted horror themes that whizzes by. There's a battle system that feels fresh and doesn't outstay its welcome. There's a hypnotic soundtrack that lingers in memory long after stopping playing. And it's all wrapped up in a presentation that has the utmost adoration and love of mid-late 90s hybrid 2D and 3D games.

Enjoy it for what it is and have fun.

Everyone mentions this game takes inspiration from Persona.  However, just as important this game takes inspiration from B movie horror.  Normal reference humor works like this, a work will go "Remember this piece of media that's superior to us?" And the audience is supposed to go "yeah I do." Demonschool does the opposite, it says "Remember this obscure terrible film?" And you say "No one remembers that, you made it up." But it turns out they didn't make it up. They've got full on reviews of bad movies in this game.  Full points for originality as far as the writing goes.

I also see people say this game is easy.  But easy how?  If all you want to do is barely scrape by to get to an ending, sure the game is easy.  But if you want to ace every map and max all the friendships between different party members, you will be swapping characters and redoing levels constantly. I really don't see this self imposed limitation as any different than picking a difficulty setting.

I can't really reiterate enough that you must enjoy the combat to enjoy the game. There are a *lot* of battles, though many of them are technically optional. They're pretty short - most battles have a time aspiration of 3-4 turns outside of boss battles, but almost every quest, sidequest and personal quest will end in a battle (and sometimes more than one). The combat system is quite fun, but after over a 100 of them they do start to wear out their welcome.

The plot and humor are serviceable but nothing amazing. There are also some minor QoL stuff that I found annoying, such as not being able to press up on the save screen to select the oldest save. Ultimately though it's all ends up as a framing device for playing the combat game.

I like this game, but I wish I loved it. Weak writing and some gameplay issues betray the stellar graphics, bumping OST, and fun tactical combat with incredible boss fights. Honestly, Demonschool leaves a terrible first impression--the earliest parts of the game are particularly rote, with sidequests like "Find a guy's sandwich," and they don't get much better from there.

In terms of characters, I quite enjoyed Faye's manic positivity and Namako's sharp uncertainty. Our protagonists are multifaceted and charming. The same can't be said for a good half of the other party members, unfortunately, who live and die by their singular joke. Destin won't shut up about snakes. Primrose keeps bringing up spleens. Jem is the worst and he keeps talking about smoochies. I do not want smoochies. I am not amused. 

I think the reason so many of the party members are one-note is that there's *so many* of them. That's great for gameplay, bad for the story. Characters will come into the plot at random with zero fanfare to join the team, because, well, they're here now, and that's what matters I guess. The male characters are the worst about this, but honestly, the male characters in general are kind of a dumping ground for the game's worst writing (again, Destin and Jem.)

The plot itself is... Fine? I went "That's it?" at the ending(s), but a big part of that comes from the fact the developers killed the plot momentum after the final boss by having all the characters stand around and pick what ending you get. I like the joke endings, they're cute, but the impact of any one was sucked out after going through ten others. I'd call it horribly indecisive on the part of the developers.

Besides the writing, there's way too much combat, but I liked the combat, so that was mostly fine. It just got a bit silly when literally every scene would have some weak excuse for fighting demons. The demons are going to attack *insert innocent person or creature* we have to help them! Okay, that's understandable, we're heroes. It's something else when we're picking flowers or trying to fix up a game console and enemies will go "I'm going to kill you for no reason because I'm evil!" but most of the enemies who do that are cops so I guess that's accurate.

Too much combat, too many party members. With a less bloated cast, they could've been setup and developed the characters (and plot) with more care. Agh, though, for as much as I've picked at this game's flaws, I do it with a weird sort of affection. I don't dislike Demonschool, I promise, I recommend the game, I just wish it was better. I can see the potential! It's SO close.

Young adults fighting demons never gets old, and this game blends both old and new ideas for the concept into a great ride. Your semester on Hemsk Island has lovable characters, witty world building, and plenty of fun distractions. The story takes you through its goofy cliches here, gripping discoveries and twists there, all presented with smooth tunes and sleek art direction. Combat is the highlight though: Don't mistake it for typical tactical RPG fare. Your teammates are basically customizeable chess pieces and each fight feels like a mini puzzle that keeps throwing in new party members and enemies to keep things fresh. There's no real dungeon crawling or major sidequests outside textboxes, but Demonschool succeeds at what it has to offer, and it's a nostalgic yet fresh way to get in some extracurricular exorcism.

Demonschool is stylish and irreverent. Grotesque foes are contrasted by the bright hues and neon stylings akin to a retrowave album cover, and the shifting electronic soundscape enhances the mood in any given scene. There are some minor pitfalls in terms of battle difficulty, but there’s enough depth and visual flair to keep things interesting. Demonschool is positively bursting with heart and energy.

Simple on paper, but once you start getting more party members, more skills to customize how they work, and more enemy variety there's a lot of interesting variety.

My only issue is that the game feels *too* long, and I personally started to fall off of it. I think it's a pacing issue - new party members & mechanics take just long enough to roll out that things could feel a bit repetitive. If, like me, your biggest touchstones to this game’s inspirations are the Persona series (post-Persona 2 duology), it’s a nice change of pace to have a main character whose background is more than just “normal person shows up at a new school, and weird stuff starts happening”. Don’t get me wrong, Faye DOES show up at a new school, and weird stuff DOES start happening, but she is far from normal, and that is AWESOME. I loved playing as the weird kid, instead of the normie who learns about everything from the weird kid.

Instead of the traditional, RPG leveling system, Demonschool has a very unique “equipment” system in place. Equipment pieces are separated into two types: Abilities and Shifts. Abilities can add to your attacks (like adding Stun or Fire), negate a character’s weaknesses (or even make them impervious to fire or poison), or (in some cases) change a character’s weapon, whereas Shifts primarily deal with movement or health. Like weaknesses and resistances, each character has their own movement pattern, their own attacking style, with the pieces of equipment giving you the ability to shape your team in almost any way you want. Personally, my Faye has a Shift assigned that allows her to teleport from one side of the battle grid to the other, if she hits the edge. Another character (no spoilers) has 2 Abilities assigned; One that adds Fire to their attacks, leaving enemies that are hit burning, with the flames jumping to neighboring enemies every turn, and another that makes Fire heal them for 1 HP instead of doing damage. Necrosoft has done a great job at making each character feel unique, with their own personalities and quirks, and the social links (for lack of a better term) to build up your relationships are an even brighter spot in a game full of bright spots. 

I absolutely love social links in my games, and Demonschool does not disappoint. Each of their stories feel very personal to them, and none of them will make you dread spending time with them, like a certain… “Gourmet King” in some other game… (fade in a picture of the fat kid from Persona 3)

Lost media buff Knute has you chasing after a mythical VHS tape, himbo Destin’s fear of a snake uprising leads to the two of you hunting down giant snakemen, and Namako gets caught up being a wedding photographer, with a whole host of others to discover. In addition to learning more about each person, these links also help the player get to know more about Faye, who shares bits of her life story with her friends while growing closer. Plus, as you wander around the town, you’ll interact with a ton of locals, each with their own wants and worries. 

As much praise as I’ve been lobbing onto the game (and it’s definitely warranted), I do have some hang-ups. The biggest would have to be the minigames Necrosoft has added into the game. There’s nothing WRONG with them per se - they’re fun bits of QTE distractions, and they’re going to be your primary way of building your relationships. You can take Knute out for some karaoke, where you have to use a specific words in all of your lyrics, or or you can cook a nice meal for Namako, matching symbols with a recipe to get it right, and as long as you don’t fail it, you’ll raise that little relationship meter, getting you closer and closer to those breakthrough social link missions.

But, outside of those relationship boosts, there doesn’t seem to be any other reason for them, other than to say “Hey, we have minigames.” Fishing has a side mission attached to it, and you do get an achievement for catching them all, but it’s just a solo endeavor. Beetle racing is there sometimes, and you even have the option to cheat at it, but there’s nothing gained from it. You don’t get any sort of combat boosts, no additional perks in fights for maxing out a relationship, nothing changes in the world if you catch every fish or win a beetle race without cheating, it’s all just… there.

I hate to compare this game directly to anything else, but my mind immediately goes to Persona 5, and its social links/minigames. Ranking up a character’s friendship will net you some sort of rewards, like the ability to Baton Pass, and playing minigames with them can raise your Technical Rank, which bumps up the damage you do to enemies hit with Technical hits. Fishing nets (pun 100% intended) you points (dependent on what you catch) which you can trade in for equipment or Velvet Room materials. This gives you more incentive to spend the time with characters, play the minigames, and feel like you’re doing it for a reason. Maybe Necrosoft could have added some higher tier equipment, specific to a character, that you can only get when you max out their friendship, or even a damage bump to your combo moves, just something outside of the (admittedly adorable) smooching scene you can get. As it stands, if you’re not into building those relationships, the minigames don’t offer up a reason to play them more than once.

Outside of these minigame thoughts, and a few bugs I ran into with the review build that were already cleared up with updates, I don’t really have any complaints. The gameplay loop is really fun, with enough variety to keep each week in-game feeling fresh. The story has plenty of twists and turns, with challenges popping up that will keep you on your toes. Oh, and, don’t sleep on the credits. Demonschool has some of the best credits I’ve ever seen in a game. Everyone from each team is named, alongside their role on the team, event staff, localization teams, but - most impressive - a lot of people on the team have what they specifically worked on listed out. It sets a new standard for game credits, in my opinion.

Demon School is absolute peak for my tastes.. it's basically an alternate-timeline Persona 3 in spirit, but it never feels derivative of persona the way you might expect... The story and characters are incredibly well executed, especially for an indie game. It's well written, and the way Faye bounces off each of her friends gives the whole cast a charm and sense of personality that’s really fun to engage with.  Faye actually makes for a perfect lead. She feels like the player… she takes everything in stride, buys into every conspiracy and ghost story, and just accepts the world for what it is under the surface. Most games would make the player-character the skeptic, but the opposite works beautifully here. It mirrors the player’s expectations. The game leans into that, and it’s clever. Having Namako as Faye's skeptical foil is perfect, and the rest of the cast supports that dynamic really well.  The Narrative really opens up a few weeks into the game with new additions to the cast of characters rolling in constantly. 

The music is incredible. There isn’t a single track that isn’t dripping with mysterious retro vibes. Every piece nails the mood.  It’s funky, retro, spooky, and ridiculously catchy. Each day of the week even has its own musical theme, and I find myself getting excited every time they're about to roll around again.

Combat is a lot of fun. It reminds me of Into the Breach, but I like it more. Planning your entire turn, sharing action points between the whole party, then watching the whole plan unfold… it’s a super satisfying loop. The shared AP turns every turn into a little puzzle. Characters like Namako, who can shove enemies around and apply weakness states, make the player feel like a genius when used well. Understanding your party, their moves, and how to set up combos allows for expressive play that feels great. It feels more like a turn based dance, it's a lot of fun.  Researching upgrades that substantially augment the way your characters function as well allows for a lot of variation despite there being no traditional xp based levelups.

And the visuals… The pixel textures, the lighting, the color work… it’s dreamy, foreboding, nostalgic, and gorgeous.  Every area in the game is densely packed with environmental detail and storytelling.  There's day/evening/night lighting and color profiles for each area that change their mood substantially.  It’s absolutely dripping with style and personality, a perfect reflection of the game’s whole vibe.

Demon School really does feel like a refined retro Persona visually, it has all teh Saturn/PSX era charm with modern post and lighting.  It's beautiful.  At the same time, it's not just an "indie Persona" it's quite unique and has it's own great mechanical ideas that set it apart.

Demonschool will land for you based on the following two criteria
- The battle system is of the tactical and deterministic variety; it has it's own quirks and challenges that are unlike many of the touchstones people may be familiar with when it comes to games it visually resembles (your Personas, your Disgaeas) and leans more into your brain boiler chess puzzle challenges (Tactical Breach Wizards, Into the Breach, and Fights in Tight Spaces are good comparisons here). No RNG, things are predictable and quickly resettable to get your ideal outcomes. It's easy to judge if you'll like this from watching the Gameplay trailer but you shouldn't go in expecting huge numbers and grindable JRPG battles
- The writing is Saturday Morning Cartoon vibes and delivered at a pace that does not have time to wait around. This is a good thing if you're after something that will make you laugh and be entertaining, but you're probably not going to get something of deep meaning out of it; it's teenagers kicking demons while the world goes to hell around them over a few weeks with no time to waste. Every character wears their emotions on their sleeves with the subtlety of a brick through the window and development, growth, and reflection aren't on the agenda for writing that's going for that Twenty Minute For A TV Episode vibe. It's closest narrative comparisons is going to be something like Night in the Woods, and really the best way to check if you'll like this is to watch the first few minutes of the story play through on a commentary free Let's Play because it maintains it's style and delivery consistently throughout. Some people will bounce here, because it's going to be hit or miss.

Should both of those be things you're fine with (or, hopefully, looking for), then rest assured that Demonschool is a riot. The game has no time to mess about with physically navigating the island or the school or physically travelling from one place to another; it moves straight from dialogue to combat and back again as fast as you can read, menu, and figure out the combat. The systems at play are on the surface simplistic but then become fierce exercises in logic that can have you analysing your party and abilities for minutes before the combat starts, reworking and restarting combats to chase that perfect grade. It's sidequests are cosy and short, it's minigames are single button input things, but you're here for watching students kick demons in the face and everything is in service to that. The music has an earworm quality to it that will be stuck in my mind for a few weeks to come, I'm sure, and the visual presentation is stunning.

In summary, you should buy it if you ever wanted Buffy The Vampire Slayer with Chess Puzzles

Demonschool, developed by Necrosoft Games and published by Ysbryd Games, is a strikingly distinctive tactics RPG that blends supernatural horror, campus life melodrama, and puzzle-like strategic combat into a single, stylistically bold package. Instead of following the traditional path of slow, stat-heavy strategy games, it introduces a brisker, more intuitive approach to turn-based tactics — one that feels deliberately crafted to appeal to both genre veterans and newcomers who prefer planning over micromanagement. All of this unfolds on a remote island where the ordinary life of university students collides with a hidden world of demons and rituals, creating a sharp tonal duality that defines the experience from the outset.

The narrative places players in the role of Faye, a student who unexpectedly gains the ability to see demons lurking beneath the island’s surface. Joined by an eclectic cast of classmates — each with their own personalities, eccentricities, and emotional arcs — she is drawn into a secret fight to uncover the truth behind a string of mysterious disappearances and supernatural disturbances. Rather than leaning on heavy exposition, the story unfolds through daily interactions, social events, small campus mysteries, and an assortment of quirky side quests that give the island a surprisingly lived-in feeling. These lighter school-life moments contrast sharply with the darker tone of the demon encounters, and the constant interplay between the mundane and the uncanny gives the plot a distinctive flavor.

Combat is where Demonschool makes its boldest design choices. Each encounter is divided into two phases: a planning stage where you map out movement and attacks, and an execution stage where every queued action plays out simultaneously. Positioning becomes the heart of strategy — characters hit harder when they strike from behind, benefit from setups arranged by teammates, and often rely on clever pushes, environmental hazards, or combos to deal significant damage. The ability to endlessly revise your plan during the setup phase encourages experimentation: the game wants you to try outrageous maneuvers, rethink approaches, and line up attacks until the solution clicks. Because actions are tied to movement rather than fixed ability lists, combat feels almost like solving a spatial puzzle where foresight matters more than raw power.

As the campaign progresses, battles introduce more variables — enemies with area-denial moves, environmental hazards, multi-wave fights, and maps that challenge the player to rethink how to manipulate space. Yet despite this escalation, the game refuses to drown the player in complexity. Damage numbers stay readable, party size remains manageable, and the planning system eliminates the frustration of committing to a mistake too early. This streamlined philosophy makes Demonschool surprisingly accessible while still offering enough tactical nuance for players who enjoy squeezing the most out of every action. When everything aligns perfectly — positioning, timing, and teamwork — the resulting chain reactions can feel immensely satisfying.

Outside combat, Demonschool’s presentation does a great deal of heavy lifting. The art direction mixes retro-inspired sprites with moody lighting and a color palette that shifts between warm campus tones and eerie supernatural hues. Character designs are expressive and memorable, leaning into the charm of 80s and 90s horror-anime aesthetics without feeling derivative. The soundtrack adds even more personality: brooding synths for demon encounters, airy melodies for campus scenes, and energetic tracks for more intense sequences. Together, these elements create a cohesive atmosphere that balances tension with levity and makes the island feel both unsettling and strangely inviting.

Despite its strong identity, Demonschool does have limitations that some players may notice. The simplicity of its core mechanics, while refreshing, can lead to a sense of repetition during longer play sessions, especially for those who crave deep customization or dense systems. The story — though engaging and stylish — sometimes leaves threads underdeveloped or relies on pacing beats that feel stretched. A few technical issues and performance inconsistencies have been reported as well, depending on platform and settings, though none fundamentally undermine the experience. Still, these rough edges reflect the challenge of balancing an ambitious mix of genres within a streamlined framework.

Taken as a whole, Demonschool stands out as an inventive and atmospheric tactics RPG that embraces accessibility without sacrificing personality. It offers a captivating blend of horror-themed combat encounters, quirky student-life interactions, and stylish presentation that give it a voice very much its own. For players interested in a tactics game that feels fresh, fast, and thoughtfully designed — or for those who enjoy the intersection of supernatural storytelling and character-driven drama — Demonschool delivers a memorable, cleverly constructed adventure that rewards observation, experimentation, and a willingness to explore the strange world hidden just beneath campus life.

Demonschool is a wonderful little horror-comedy flick rolled up in the form of a tactics RPG. It's writing never lacks wit, and the dumbass college kids could always get a chuckle out of me. That being said, I think the game kind of suffers from having way too many characters in its main cast. Still, I can't deny that Demonschool has been one of my favorite games of 2025.

Gameplay wise, I'm certainly not the best judge of nuance with a history of tactical RPGs that numbers 1 (Final Fantasy Tactics). Still, the combat puzzles laid out before you tend to stay fresh and fun with a few interesting gimmicks thrown into the mix (explosives-heavy levels or ghosts that force you to better manage your space). It felt incredibly stylish as well, and the visuals on display were always striking, especially with team-up attacks.

In fact, some of the UI and art design reminded me a little bit of Paradise Killer in the best of ways. It's a small thing, but UI with a strong enough sense of intent and design behind it can help cultivate a visual style, and I think Necrosoft Games pulled it off with flying colors.

As for the characters themselves, I think they can be Demonschool's weakest link. It simply feels like the cast is far too large. This then has the unfortunate side-effect of making each character's relationship missions feel so much more brief and lacking in breadth. I wish I had gotten a lot more time with many of the earlier characters, rather than carrying an ever-growing roster of characters that were sometimes felt only distinguished from one another by their special ability. That being said, none of the characters were bad per se. Just that a few felt shallow and/or out of place.

All in all though, Demonschool is a worthwhile play. It knows that it's here for its tactics gameplay, and its level design never felt poor, too difficult, or indecipherable.

In addition, the game starts to rapidly introduce new combat mechanics near the tail-end of the story without giving the player a chance to really adjust to it in any meaningful way. Again, not going into specifics for spoilers, but it happens fairly frequently and then is promptly never touched again.

The story starts off very strongly. The initial few weeks feel very solid, and, without spoilers, most of the initial party feel as if they have a lot of chemistry in the way they interact, and all react to the situations presented before them very organically. As the story progresses, more party members get introduced, and it's clear the game doesn't know what to do with them. As well, the later-introduction party members are given little-to-no development, even within their Companion Quests. In any given scene, members of the party are either present without dialogue, or simply just not present whatsoever, even in seemingly important story scenes. - The combat is fun for a while. Think Into the Breach but with college kids in the 90's instead of mechs.
- The music is nice, and the aesthetic/artwork/character designs are very good.

The So-So:
- Extremely linear. I don't mind this once in a while, but if you're into exploration - this ain't it.
- Really light on RPG elements. If you like min/maxing, like I do, this is kiddie pool level shallow. But, some might like that its not overly complicated in this area.
- Without spoilers, the overarching story is very basic. Any RPG player has played through this sort of story dozens of times. Generally, this isn't a problem but...

The Bad:
- The writing is atrocious. This is the biggest reason I can't recommend, because you need to have strong writing in narrative heavy RPGs (sort of the point, no?). This is a prime example of insufferable millennial theater kid style writing (best way I can describe it; make of that what you will). Every character tries to be funny, and none of them are. Everybody's so quirky and cool! How fun! (extreme sarcasm) They're all supposed to be college students, but they act like i-pad kids hopped up on sugar (the main protagonist being one of the worst of the bunch, so the cringe train never stops). There's little to no character development, and at no point in the 30 hours of the story did I once give a fudge about any of them (and there's like 15 of 'em). 

- The combat: while its also in the Good section, the game doesn't keep it interesting enough. All RPG combat systems become repetitive at some point - but this one overstays its welcome much earlier than most. This is due to a lack of enemy variety, and every fight (outside of a handful) being in the exact same arena. Compound that with the game insisting on punctuating every single story beat, side or main, with a fight (sometimes up to three straight), and it drains on your patience really fast. This problem only gets worse as you get deeper into the game.

The grading system for combat also falls flat. It's fun to try to complete the fights in the allotted number of turns for a while, but without an incentive to do so (coupled with the repetitiveness and frequency of the fights), the whole system becomes inconsequential. You DO get more currency to use if you get A rank - but I had thousands leftover at the end of the game - and I researched and bought everything possible. The last maybe 10 hours or so I just played like a donkey to get it over with instead of actually trying to be strategic and shoot for that 'A' (although, the games not exactly hard; so you can still donk and get A's for days).

- The relationship stuff: wouldn't be a Persona-like game without this feature. Difference here, compared to Persona, is the characters mostly suck, and their side-stories suck just as much. You aren't getting anything emotional or compelling out of these relationship building portions of the game. Outside of unlocking a passive to research at the end of the relationship, there is no other benefit to raising relationship levels with the characters. Persona, on the other hand, seamlessly intertwines the relationship mechanic with the combat and dungeon crawling aspects of the game.

4/10
